title: Pipkin and Bartholomew's Brave New Chart
markdown:
Willowbrook was a village so neat you could eat off the pavement, which nobody did, because of the pavement. There lived Pipkin, the dentist's assistant, who had noticed something important: the children were terrified of Dr. Gnash's chomping chair.

"This won't do," Pipkin declared. He put on his thinking cap and rummaged his treasure chest for glitter and sharp crayons. Thus the Willowbrook Bravery Chart — not mere paper, a map to courage. Every time a child sat still or managed a tiny nervous smile, Pipkin awarded a golden star. Soon the clinic walls dazzled with sparkly grins and stickers. Absolutely marvelous, if you liked that sort of enamel parade.

Deep in the whispering woods lived Kit the badger, Della the terrier, and Professor Pine the owl. Kit loved collecting stars. Della wondered what truly made a smile brave. Professor Pine called it a fascinating deviation from the norm, which was owl for he wanted a closer look.

Then, one blustery afternoon, Bartholomew Higgins stomped into Willowbrook. He was a mole whose disposition was as sour as old jam, and he detested the cheerful commotion.

"Smiling? It's a sham," he grumbled, nose twitching. "Real bravery is quiet. It's deep down."

Kit, confused, puffed out his chest and offered his biggest star-worthy grin. Della noticed it did not budge Bartholomew's face. Professor Pine inquired, politely, after his name and his thoughts on the custom.

"Bartholomew Higgins," he huffed, dry leaves. "This village has gone daft about teeth. Bravery is facing the dark, not flaunting enamel."

Kit and Della exchanged glances. Unmoved. Then Bartholomew sighed, like wind through a log, and his gruffness thinned.

"Look. I'm just… not good at smiling. People stare. So I decided it was easier not to. I hide when it comes to cheerful displays. I spend my days digging, dark and damp. That's brave, isn't it? Nobody gives you a sticker for it."

Pipkin, who had joined the huddle, felt his kind heart somersault. "Mr. Higgins. You're absolutely right. Bravery comes in shapes. Digging deep takes courage. Perhaps yours needs a different spotlight."

He held out blank paper. "We have a Bravery Chart. The village could use charts for Kindness. Listening. Thoughtfulness. With your knowledge of the deep and the quiet, and that excellent nose for what matters — would you help design them?"

Bartholomew blinked. He had never been asked for his opinion. He looked at Pipkin, at Kit and Della, at Professor Pine, who nodded as if the deviation had become data. He took a breath. Slowly his lips curved — not a wide grin, a small wobbly thing, like a sprout through hard ground. But it was a smile.

Villagers gasped, then cheered, because Willowbrook never did anything by halves. Pipkin beamed and reached not for a sticker but a tiny golden crayon. Beside Bartholomew's name he drew a determined sprout.

Dr. Gnash's chair still chomped. The stars still shone for those who sat in it. There was, now, a second chart in the making, for work nobody clapped at until a mole said it out loud.

Bartholomew wondered, pocketing a spare crayon as if it might bite, whether underground bravery would need glow-in-the-dark ink — and whether Pipkin would let him test that theory far from the chomping chair, which even a mole of principle preferred to visit only when strictly necessary.
